name: Ada Brockway
languages: French (from her father's partner, a Canadian voyageur)
equipment: Buckskin coat, smoke-tanned, lined with a striped trade blanket, over a man's wool shirt and canvas trousers
Repeating rifle (a Henry, .44 rimfire, brass frame worn bright at the wrist), 12 in the magazine, in a fringed saddle scabbard
Field glasses in a leather case, French, bought from a Boise gambler who needed the money more than the view
Pick and pan, a horn spoon and a gold scale with brass weights
A poke of gold dust, about four ounces, from her own claim on the Upper Bench, which pays wages and not much more
A claim paper for Number Nine Above Discovery, Upper Bench, Ninebark district, recorded 3 August 1864
Snowshoes (Canadian bearpaw pattern) and a pair of wool socks for every day of the week
Horse: Biscuit, a dun mountain pony with a black stripe down his back and no fear of anything but water
A pack mule called Judge, who carries her tent, a Dutch oven and her winter flour
Bedroll, canteen, matches in a corked bottle
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saves against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; needs half the usual water one day in three; once per long rest she can shrug off a level of exhaustion gained on the trail)

Trailcraft (Scout: never lost on terrain she has crossed, by day or night; finds water every day without a check where any exists within a day's travel; follows a trail at normal pace with a Survival check and learns how many riders, how long ago, and whether the horses were shod, loaded or lame)
Long Shot (Scout: no disadvantage at long range with a Longarm if she Aimed first this turn; proficiency bonus doubled on Perception to spot something more than 300 ft away)

Ghost on the Range (Scout, 2nd level: in natural terrain she can Hide as a bonus action and hide when only lightly obscured; normal travel pace does not impose disadvantage on Stealth; she leaves no trail that anyone without Trailcraft can follow unless she chooses)

Path: Guide (Scout, 3rd level: her party travels at a hard pace without exhaustion, finds forage for its horses on any terrain that has any, and has advantage on saves against weather; in a Montana December this is worth more than the rifle)

Color in the Creek (Prospector background: she tells good ore from bad without a check, finds the recorder, the assayer and the claim jumpers within an hour of arriving, and knows which strikes are salted; miners share a fire and a rumour with her)

personality.traits: I say less than I see. I would rather sleep out than in a hotel. I laugh at the wrong moments, loudly, and I am not sorry.
personality.ideals: The country does not care who you are, and that is the only fair thing about it. People ought to try to be as fair as the weather.
personality.bonds: My claim on the Upper Bench, which is mine because I staked it and the miners' meeting recorded it, and nobody has yet found a way to say a woman can't. And Moira Kehoe, who nursed me through the mountain fever in September and whose husband the committee hanged.
personality.flaws: I trust tracks more than people. When the tracks and the people disagree I stop listening to the people, and I have been wrong that way before.

appearance: A tall, rangy woman of twenty-one, sunburnt even in November, with straw-coloured hair cropped short under a battered slouch hat, a wide mouth and grey eyes that crinkle into a squint when she looks at anything farther than a hundred yards. Moves quietly and sits on her heels by a fire like a man who has done it all his life.
backstory: Ada Brockway was born in a wagon on the Oregon Trail in 1843, on the Sweetwater, and raised on a claim on the Columbia and then in the mining camps of the Idaho country, where her father prospected and her mother kept a boarding tent and the family's money. She learned to track from her father's partner, a Canadian voyageur who had trapped every river from the Saskatchewan to the Snake, and to shoot from necessity. When her father died in the Boise Basin in 1863 she buried him, sold the boarding tent, bought a Henry rifle and a mule, and came over the mountains to the new strikes. She has a claim on the Upper Bench above Ninebark and knows the gulches, the side canyons and the passes better than anyone in camp, including the road agents, which is a thing she has begun to suspect. On the night of 10 November she saw the committee walk Patrick Kehoe down the gulch to the slaughter corral, forty masked men with lanterns, and could not think of a single thing to do. She has not forgiven herself. (Suggested hook: Moira Kehoe asks her to find out who really robbed the coaches; or Simeon Prothero hires her to read the sign after Thursday's robbery.)
